title: Weekly toolbox talks and safety alerts
audience: Supervisors and leads who run short safety talks with their crews and post safety information at sites.
learningOutcomes: Plan and run a short weekly toolbox talk that a crew can take part in.
Choose and post a safety alert that suits the sites the crew works on.
Record attendance, topics and actions from each talk.

instruction.heading: Why a short regular talk helps
instruction.body: In the sample, a weekly safety meeting is run on each work site by the supervisor, with a senior operations deputy plus a safety officer, while the training lead also attends. The purpose is to keep everyone informed of changes that affect their safety and wellbeing. A talk of ten to fifteen minutes, held on a fixed day each week, works well for a crew because it is regular and focused. It also gives workers a place to raise hazards they have noticed.

instruction.heading: Choosing topics and alerts
instruction.body: Choose a topic from the week's real work: a chemical that was used more, a near miss, a change to a method, or a hazard seen on a site. The sample also posts weekly safety and health alerts on work sites, drawn from internal and external material where management judges them relevant. Use alerts that match what the crew actually does. A generic alert that is never connected to the work is quickly ignored.

instruction.heading: Recording the talk and following up
instruction.body: Record the date, the site, the people present, the topic and any action agreed. An action might be a change to a procedure, a request for equipment, or a report to the manager. Check at the next talk whether the action was completed. The sample does not set legal requirements for these talks. Check whether a weekly talk meets the consultation duties that apply under Australian WHS law. See “WHS duties and consultation” for the consultation duties and check the local arrangements.

procedure: Pick one topic linked to the week's work, such as a method change or a hazard seen on site.
Hold the talk at the agreed time, keeping it to ten to fifteen minutes, with each attendee given a chance to speak.
Choose a matching safety alert and post it at the site where the crew can see it.
Record the date, site, attendees, topic and any action agreed.
At the next talk, report whether each action was completed and close the ones that were.

workedExamples.situation: After a worker reported splashing a strong cleaning product during a sink clean, a crew lead on a commercial site plans the next toolbox talk.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the talk cover, which alert should be posted, and what record should be kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: The talk covers how the product should be used and the steps to take after a splash, based on the product's own instructions and the site procedure. The alert matches the topic. The record shows the names present, the action agreed, such as checking the storage location, and the date it is checked.

equipmentAndPpe: Attendance sheet or form. The product instructions and site procedure for any product discussed. Standard PPE on site.

commonErrors.error: Holding talks that are never recorded, so actions are lost.
commonErrors.prevention: Record every talk on the same form the same day.

commonErrors.error: Posting alerts that do not relate to the site.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose alerts that match the work the crew does.

commonErrors.error: Letting the talk become a long meeting.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep to a short, fixed slot with one topic.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Consultation duties and the form of safety talks depend on the workplace and the law. See “WHS duties and consultation”.

qualityStandard: Each talk has a record with date, site, attendees, topic and action.
Each action is checked at the next talk and marked closed or carried forward.
documentationEvidence: Toolbox talk record with attendees, topic and action.
Copy of the posted safety alert with the posting date.
summary: A short, regular talk keeps the crew informed and gives a place to raise hazards.
Choose topics and alerts that match the work actually done.
Record every talk and check each action at the next one.

knowledgeChecks.question: What makes a toolbox talk useful for a crew?
options: It is brief, regular and tied to the work itself
It runs for two hours each month with lunch
It is held only when a client complains
It replaces every written procedure for the site

knowledgeChecks.question: Which alert best suits a crew that works on a commercial site?
options: A generic alert unrelated to the work for any crew
An alert on a hazard the crew meets in its own work
An alert about a different industry and its own rules
No alert at all on the site or in the van today

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a supervisor do with an action agreed at a toolbox talk?
options: Forget it unless someone asks at the next talk
Leave it to the crew to remember and tell nobody
Record it and check its status at the next talk
Report it only to the client on the next visit
